lead: Light moves at 3.00×10⁸ m/s in vacuum. That number comes out the same for a person on a platform and for a passenger in a train rushing past the lamp. Ordinary velocity addition cannot deliver that. Special relativity keeps c fixed and lets space and time adjust instead: a moving clock runs slow by the factor γ, and a moving rod shortens along its motion. GPS satellites, particle accelerators and cosmic-ray muons all depend on these corrections. Only a few universities teach this inside the mechanics unit.
prereq: You need 1.1 for inertial frames and Galilean velocity addition.

sections.h3: Inertial frames and the failure of Galilean addition

blocks.text: An inertial frame is one in which a body with no net force keeps a constant velocity (1.1). Two inertial frames moving at relative speed v compare positions through the Galilean transformation x′ = x − vt, where x is a position, t is the time and v is the frame speed. Velocities then subtract: u′ = u − v. A ball thrown at 10 m/s inside a train moving at 20 m/s travels at 30 m/s for the ground observer.

Light was expected to obey the same rule, travelling through a space-filling medium called the ether. Michelson and Morley split a beam, sent the two halves along perpendicular arms, and recombined them into fringes. An ether wind blowing along one arm would delay that beam. Rotating the whole apparatus by 90° swaps the arms, so the fringes should shift. No shift was ever seen. The ether wind does not exist, and the ether was dropped from physics.
Einstein replaced the ether with two postulates.

items: The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame. No frame is special.
Light in vacuum travels at c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of the source or of the observer.

blocks.text: The second postulate destroys absolute simultaneity. A lamp flashes at the centre of a moving coach. The passenger sees both ends lit together. A ground observer sees the rear wall move into the light and the front wall move away, so the rear is lit first. Both are correct: “at the same time” depends on the frame.

blocks.where: γ (gamma) is the Lorentz factor, a pure number; v is the relative speed of the two frames and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s. γ = 1 at rest, and γ grows without limit as v → c.

Δt is the time between two events measured in a frame where the clock moves; Δτ is the proper time, read by a clock present at both events. Proper time is the shortest time between those events, so you multiply it by γ, never divide.
L₀ is the proper length, measured in the object's rest frame; L is the length measured in a frame moving at v along the object. Only the dimension along the motion shrinks.

items: Velocities do not simply add: u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²). Put u′ = c and you get u = c again, as the postulate demands.
Coordinates mix: x′ = γ(x − vt) and t′ = γ(t − vx/c²).
The interval s² = c²t² − x² is the same in every inertial frame. It is the one quantity all observers agree on.
Momentum is p = γmv and energy is E = γmc². At rest this leaves E = mc², the rest energy.

figure.caption: γ hugs 1 at everyday speeds and climbs steeply as v approaches c. The marked point is the muon of the worked example, at v = 0.98c with γ = 5.03.

spec.aria: A plot of the Lorentz factor against v/c: it stays close to 1 at everyday speeds and rises steeply as v approaches c, with the muon's point marked at 0.98c and 5.03.

examples.question: A muon is created 3.0 km above sea level and falls straight down at v = 0.98c. Its proper lifetime is 2.2 μs. Take c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s. Find γ, the lifetime measured in the lab, and the distance travelled. Compare with the distance travelled if time dilation did not exist.
steps: The proper time is Δτ = 2.2 μs, so the lab lifetime is Δt = γΔτ = 5.03 × 2.2 μs = 11.1 μs, i.e. 11.1×10⁻⁶ s.
Distance in the lab = vΔt = 2.94×10⁸ × 11.1×10⁻⁶ = 3.25×10³ m.
Without dilation the muon would live 2.2 μs and cover 2.94×10⁸ × 2.2×10⁻⁶ = 647 m.
examples.answer: γ = 5.03, the lab lifetime is 11.1 μs, and the muon covers 3.25×10³ m instead of 647 m, so it reaches the ground from 3.0 km.
examples.check:
import math
c = 3.00e8
v = 0.98*c
tau = 2.2e-6
gamma = 1/math.sqrt(1-(v/c)**2)
dt = gamma*tau
d = v*dt
d0 = v*tau
print(round(gamma,2))
print(round(dt*1e6,1))
print(round(d))
print(round(d0))

traps: Proper time is the shortest time between two events: Δt = γΔτ. Dividing by γ instead of multiplying gives a lifetime shorter than the rest-frame one, which is impossible.
Length contraction acts only along the direction of motion. A moving sphere flattens along v but keeps its full width across v; students often shrink all three dimensions.
γ uses v, the relative speed of the two frames. In glass light travels slower than c, but the c written in every relativity formula is still 3.00×10⁸ m/s.
A question about “the length of the train” is incomplete until it names the frame. Lengths and time gaps are frame-dependent; only c and the interval s² are shared.
γ is never less than 1, so the dilated time is always longer and the contracted length always shorter. Any answer that breaks this is a sign error.

quiz.q: State the two postulates of special relativity.
quiz.a: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Light in vacuum has speed c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s for every inertial observer, independent of the motion of source or observer.

quiz.q: Why did the Michelson–Morley experiment give no fringe shift when the apparatus was turned by 90°, and what idea was dropped because of it?
quiz.a: An ether wind along one arm would delay that beam, and turning the apparatus would move the delay to the other arm, shifting the fringes. No shift was seen, so there is no ether wind: light's speed does not depend on the observer's motion through space. The ether was dropped.

quiz.q: A spacecraft passes Earth at v = 0.6c. A clock inside it ticks 1.00 s between two events. What does Earth measure for that interval, and what is γ?
quiz.a: v/c = 0.6, so v²/c² = 0.36 and 1 − 0.36 = 0.64. γ = 1/√0.64 = 1/0.8 = 1.25. Δt = γΔτ = 1.25 × 1.00 s = 1.25 s. Earth measures a longer interval, as it must.

quiz.q: A rod of proper length 2.00 m moves at v = 0.6c along its own length. What length does the lab measure, and what is its width across the motion?
quiz.a: γ = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 2.00/1.25 = 1.60 m. The width across the motion is unchanged.

quiz.q: A muon is created high in the atmosphere and reaches the ground although its proper lifetime times c is shorter than the height. Explain this from the ground frame and from the muon frame, and show the two answers agree.
quiz.a: Ground frame: the muon's clock runs slow, so the lifetime is γΔτ and the distance is vγΔτ. Muon frame: the muon lives Δτ, but the atmosphere is a moving object of contracted length h/γ, and h/γ = vΔτ is the same condition. Both frames predict the same meeting of muon and ground, because that meeting is one event.

quiz.q: What is the spacetime interval s² = c²t² − x², and why is it more useful than t or x alone?
quiz.a: It is a combination of a time gap and a distance gap between two events. Every inertial frame computes the same value for it, so it plays the role that distance plays in ordinary geometry. Frames disagree on t and x but never on s².

beyond: Not for the exam. GPS clocks need about 38 μs a day of net correction, and the position fix drifts within minutes if it is skipped. Accelerator designers use γ daily to relate magnet settings to particle momentum, since p = γmv. Relativistic Doppler shift explains the colour change of fast jets, and the same algebra leads into general relativity, where gravity bends time as well. Search for “Lorentz transformation four-vector” and “relativistic Doppler effect” next.
